q: Which of these should you catch?
options: A bug in your own code
A file that is not there
A typo in a variable name
why: A recoverable error is a thing that goes wrong in normal operation. A bug is your program being wrong, and a traceback that stops the program is the most useful thing it can do.

q: What does the `else` clause of a `try` do?
options: Runs when an exception was caught
Runs only when no exception happened
why: It exists so the `try` can hold only the risky line, instead of quietly catching failures from everything else you put in there.

options: Replaces whatever was leaving the block, including a propagating exception
why: ruff's `B012` exists for exactly this. There is no traceback afterwards, because the traceback was discarded.

Only when no exception was raised
On every way out of the block, including a `return`
After the function returns to its caller
why: Which is what makes it right for cleanup, and a `with` statement is usually the better way to say it.

why: It is one operation rather than two, so nothing can change in between, and it is one lookup rather than two.

q: When is LBYL the better choice?
options: When the failure is expected often, or the check is much cheaper than the attempt
why: Setting up a `try` is nearly free since 3.11. Raising is not, at roughly a microsecond, which matters only in a tight loop.

q: `raise NewError(...) from exc` produces which message?
options: "The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception"
"During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred"
why: The second is what implicit chaining prints, and it reads as a second bug appearing inside your handler rather than a deliberate translation.

options: Use `raise ... from err` or `from None` when raising inside an `except`
Add a docstring to your exception
why: Losing the original is losing the only evidence of what actually went wrong.

q: To re-raise the exception you just caught, write
why: A bare `raise` re-raises the exception in flight. Naming it works too, but a bare `raise` is the form that says what you mean.

q: A class must derive from what before it can be raised?
options: Nothing; any class can be raised
why: Derive from `Exception` in practice. `except` has the same requirement, which is a second way to meet this error.
